extracted.intended_audience: science press officers, science journalists, and scientists interested in media relations
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the quality and practices of science journalism and media-relations (press officers, briefings, PR) with respect to originality, accuracy, verification, resources, and the effects of 'churnalism'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'churnalism'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Working in a news factory, without the time to check, without the chance to go out and make contacts and find leads, reporters are reduced to churnalism, to the passive processing of material which overwhelmingly tends to be supplied for them by outsiders, particularly wire agencies and PR."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterised by being too commercially driven, obsessed with speed, understaffed, and relying on externally supplied material rather than original reporting. Used as shorthand for low-effort, recycled journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story is 'truly original reporting' versus derived from wire copy or PR material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cardiff analysis cited: over 60% of stories came wholly or mainly from wire/PR, 20% contained clear elements of PR, only 12% were genuinely original. Originality is signalled by journalists digging, attending events, cultivating contacts, and producing exclusive investigations (e.g., Sunday Times Insight-style long investigations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Are stories truthful and accurate, not mere 'fabrication' of PR designed to serve an interest?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies argues 'Fabrication is at the heart of PR' while the author counters that many press officers generate real news; evaluation requires checking whether PR-originated stories are factually sound and not spin. Examples: accurate coverage by specialist reporters (Mail's science and health reporters) demonstrates accuracy is possible under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and expert scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claims have been verified and checked by independent scientific advisers or specialist journalists who interrogate experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC claims stories they offer are 'verified as significant by our many scientific advisers and written up by specialist journalists who use the briefing to interrogate the experts.' Good practice: involve expert referees, specialist reporters, and interrogation rather than uncritical repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source provenance (PR/wire dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which stories derive from wire services or PR material versus independent journalistic work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provenance metrics (e.g., Cardiff study percentages) to assess how much of the media's output is facilitated by PR/wire; high dependence is evidence of churnalism but provenance alone doesn't prove inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and resources allocated to stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of timelines and resources (days, weeks, years) to investigate stories rather than producing rapid diary copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies highlights a past 'luxurious' timeline (e.g., Sunday Times Insight) where lengthy investigations were possible. Modern reporters often handle multiple stories per day, limiting investigative depth. Assessment: whether journalists had sufficient time to verify and develop stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialist versus non-specialist reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether coverage is produced by specialist science/health reporters or by non-specialists/political/lobby correspondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that most 'terrible examples of grossly inaccurate media coverage' were written by non-specialists. Specialist reporters are more likely to produce accurate, nuanced coverage, especially on complex topics (e.g., human-animal hybrid embryos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance and engagement with events
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether journalists attend sessions, mix with scientists/audience, and seek leads rather than staying in separate press briefings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of conference practice: reporters often stay in separate buildings and attend 20-minute press briefings rather than sessions. Attendance is a signal of original reporting; reliance on press briefings suggests packaged news consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packaging (spoon-feeding) versus investigative discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which press officers or intermediaries package 'science on a plate' for fast-moving media rather than enabling investigative discovery by reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC's role described as adapting complex science to media needs; this can be seen as helpful or as 'spoon feeding' journalists. Evaluation: does packaging aid accurate communication or encourage passive reproduction of PR lines?

rubrics_metrics.name: Press officer role: generator vs spinner
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether press officers genuinely generate and facilitate real news and expert access or primarily 'spin' corporate/institutional messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues many press officers (e.g., British Veterinary Association examples) do vital work facilitating expert access during crises. Good press officers should avoid corporate spin, instead promoting truth-telling and enabling expert scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workload and multi-format demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' workload (e.g., routinely working on 2–3 stories a day and adapting them to web, podcasts, video) and its impact on quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High workload and multi-format expectations reduce time per story and can encourage churning. Exceptional journalists may still produce accurate copy under pressure; workload is a risk factor rather than deterministic proof of poor quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-skilling of journalistic work
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which journalistic craft has been de-skilled, shifting from investigative writing to churning recycled material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: 'We are churning stories today, not writing them...the work has been de-skilled.' Evaluate by looking at types of pieces produced (recycled vs investigative features) and evidence of investigative skill (sourcing, development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence that PR-originated stories are unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Need for evidence that stories facilitated by press officers and packaged for reporters are false or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author challenges Davies to show that PR-facilitated stories from SMC briefings were not 'truth-telling'; assessment requires case-by-case examination rather than assuming unreliability from provenance alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of background briefings
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether 'background' briefings (not new research) are legitimate sources for news and worthy of journalists' attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMC notes many briefings are background but still yielded stories; evaluation should consider whether such briefings help contextualise important issues and lead to accurate reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of outstanding individual journalistic skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledging that some reporters can produce high-quality output quickly (e.g., turning complex briefings into accurate 500-word stories rapidly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: John Von Radowitz producing up to ten stories per shift accurately. Assessment should distinguish systemic problems from the achievements of talented individuals.
